introduction: This intermediate tier explores the bedrock jurisprudential doctrines crafted by the Indian Supreme Court (largely spearheaded by M.C. Mehta litigations). It breaks down the shift from Strict Liability to Absolute Liability and the economic principles governing pollution.

core_concepts.title: Strict Liability vs. Absolute Liability
core_concepts.description:
- Strict Liability (*Rylands v. Fletcher*, 1868): If you bring something dangerous onto your land and it escapes, you are strictly liable. BUT, it has exceptions: Act of God, Act of Stranger, Plaintiff's fault, etc.
- Absolute Liability (*M.C. Mehta v. Union of India - Oleum Gas Leak Case*, 1987): The Supreme Court discarded the 19th-century English rule. It held that an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous industry owes an **absolute and non-delegable duty** to the community. There are **ZERO exceptions**. The enterprise must pay compensation, and the amount of compensation must correlate to the magnitude and financial capacity of the enterprise.

core_concepts.title: Polluter Pays Principle
core_concepts.description:
Adopted in the *Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996)* case (Tanneries case).
- The Rule: The absolute financial responsibility for repairing environmental damage and compensating victims lies solely with the polluter. It is not just about compensating victims, but also the cost of restoring the environmental degradation. The government/taxpayers should not bear the cost of corporate pollution.

core_concepts.title: Precautionary Principle
core_concepts.description:
Also established in the *Vellore Citizens* case.
- The Rule: The State and statutory authorities must anticipate, prevent, and attack the causes of environmental degradation. Crucially, **scientific uncertainty should NOT be used as a reason for postponing measures** to prevent environmental degradation. The burden of proof shifts to the industry to prove their actions are *not* environmentally harmful.

core_concepts.title: Public Trust Doctrine
core_concepts.description:
Adopted in *M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997)* (The Span Motel Case).
- The Doctrine: The State is a 'Trustee' of all natural resources (like rivers, forests, seashores, and air) which are meant for public use. The State cannot transfer these resources into private ownership for commercial exploitation. The resources belong to the people ('the beneficiaries').

important_entities.name: Sustainable Development
important_entities.significance: Defined by the Brundtland Report (1987) as 'development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs' (Inter-generational Equity). Indian courts use this to refuse complete bans on industry, opting instead for regulated, sustainable operations.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners will propose a scenario: 'A chemical plant leaks toxic gas due to an unprecedented earthquake. Can the company claim the Act of God exception?' **NO**. Under India's Absolute Liability rule (Oleum Gas case), there are absolutely no exceptions, not even an Act of God. The enterprise remains 100% liable.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Oleum = Absolute, Kamal Nath = Trust, Vellore = Polluter Pays
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: M.C. Mehta filed almost all landmark environmental PILs. Use these key associations to tell them apart in multiple-choice questions.

exam_strategy_tips: If a UPSC Law Optional question asks you to trace the evolution of corporate liability in environmental disasters, you MUST contrast the outdated English *Rylands v. Fletcher* rule with Chief Justice P.N. Bhagwati's indigenous **Absolute Liability** doctrine.
